name: Fatima Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I don't work for the power company itself, I work for Harlow Line Services, a private contractor the power company hires. Most weeks we're upgrading old lines round the docks and the industrial estate, swapping wooden poles for concrete ones. But when a big storm hits anywhere in the country, we pack the trucks and drive through the night to help put it back together. Storm work is where you learn the most, because nothing is where the drawings say it is.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that a contractor gets paid for results, so the quick, careful crews get the work. I use AI every day: it reads the drawings for me, helps price the side jobs I do, and keeps my budget. What wears me out is the travel and the hotel food. I share a flat with my younger sister Amira, who's at college, and I'm saving because one day I want my own small contracting firm with two trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because the tools were just getting useful. At work I'd say the crews who use them well still have an edge. I'd post a short thing on the contractors' forum I read about which tools actually stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. Line work is steady, and contractors always have a queue of jobs from the power company. My own plan doesn't depend on AI getting better, it depends on me saving and getting good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working storm call-outs because they pay double. I'd keep putting about four hundred a month into my business fund. And I'd keep doing small side jobs, like hooking up farm sheds and solar panels, priced with the AI tools I already use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little impatient, maybe, because I wanted the tools to do more of the boring office work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your own firm. How far off is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About five years, if I'm honest. A second-hand bucket truck is around forty thousand, and I've got maybe six thousand put by after my emergency money. I'd need a few big storm seasons and a bank that believes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to about that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Karim, who ran a building firm for thirty years. He says start small, never borrow for the second truck until the first one's paid for, and keep your own name on the door. I listen to him more than to any online course.

say: It's a **shame**, because the tools were just getting useful.
Crews who use the tools well **still have an edge**.
think: **Line work is steady**, and contractors always have a queue of jobs.
My plan depends on **saving and getting good**, not on AI improving.
do: Keep taking **storm call-outs**, which pay double.
Put **£400 a month** into her business fund.
Keep doing **side jobs** like farm sheds and solar hook-ups.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **impatience** about office work staying manual.
S0.quote: My own plan doesn't depend on AI getting better, it depends on me saving and getting good.
fieldNote: Fatima works for a **private contractor** and wants her own firm in about five years.
She gets business advice from her **uncle Karim**, not from courses.
She already uses AI **daily** for drawings, pricing and budgeting.

steps.text: Keep taking double-pay storm call-outs across the country
Put £400 a month into the fund for her own bucket truck
Price and do weekend farm-shed and solar hook-ups

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for small firms that move fast. On the forum I'd say the crews who learn to quote, plan and do the paperwork with AI will win the contracts. At work I'd say it more gently, because some of the older lads hate screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this suits me down to the ground. Half of what stops a lineworker starting a firm is the office side: tendering, pricing, safety paperwork, invoicing. If AI does that, a two-truck firm can bid against the big contractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own firm sooner, maybe in three years instead of five. I'd use AI tools for every bid and set up the paperwork systems now, while I'm still employed. And I'd take on more side jobs to grow the fund faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit excited. I'd be nervous about the money, but that's normal for anyone starting a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the older lads hate screens. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis, our crew boss, who's been on lines for thirty years. He's brilliant up a pole and useless on a tablet. In this picture I'd worry he loses the planning side of his job to software, and with it some of his pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you about your own work here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Contractors get squeezed first when the power company saves money. If their own AI plans jobs better, they need fewer outside crews. That's another reason I'd want my own firm, small and cheap, instead of being one of a hundred contract hands.

say: This is **good news** for small firms that move fast.
Crews who quote and **plan with AI** will win the contracts.
think: AI handling **tendering and paperwork** lets a two-truck firm bid against big contractors.
**Contractors get squeezed** first when the power company saves money.
do: Start her own firm in **three years** instead of five.
Set up **AI bidding and paperwork** systems now, while still employed.
Take on **more side jobs** to grow the fund faster.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, with normal nerves about money.
S1.quote: Half of what stops a lineworker starting a firm is the office side: tendering, pricing, safety paperwork, invoicing.
fieldNote: Fatima sees AI taking **office work** as a door opening for small firms.

Her calm rests on a **business plan**, though contractor work is the first to be squeezed.

steps.text: Set up AI bidding and invoicing templates for her future firm
Take two extra farm and solar side jobs a month
Bring her own firm's launch forward from five to three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three pictures share an end point. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who own the robots will do fine and the people who are the robots' replacement won't. At work I'd say we need to think like owners. On the forum I'd be honest that this is fast and nobody's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it messes up my timing. My firm was going to be built on my hands and a truck, and by 2031 the robots do the hands. So I'd have three years of running a firm before the thing I'm selling, line work, gets cheaper than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stop the truck plan and keep the cash. I'd look at being one of the first small firms to rent or buy a line robot when they appear, and spend the next three years getting known for quick, safe jobs. And I'd keep six months saved, because contractors get cut first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like my odds better than most, but I'm twenty-seven with six thousand pounds, and robot fleets will belong to companies with millions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone, for how fast this happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, that's how markets move. I'd blame people who sit still and expect someone else to look after them. My uncle Karim would say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister Amira the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister Amira to finish her college course but to pick something where she's working with people face to face. She's doing accountancy, which is exactly the thinking work that goes first. I'd be more worried for her than for me.

say: People who **own the robots** will do fine.
We need to **think like owners**, and nobody is ready for this speed.
think: By **2031** robots do the hands, which wrecks her firm's timing.
She'd have about **three years** before line work gets cheaper than her.
do: **Pause the truck plan** and keep the cash.
Aim to be among the first small firms to **rent a line robot**.
Keep **six months saved**, since contractors get cut first.
feel: **Anxious**, because robot fleets will belong to **firms with millions**.
S2.quote: My firm was going to be built on my hands and a truck, and by 2031 the robots do the hands.
fieldNote: Fatima shifts from building a **firm on labour** to owning machines.
She blames **no one**, seeing it as markets, and faults people who wait to be helped.
Her bigger worry is her sister Amira's **accountancy course**, high on thinking AI.

steps.text: Pause the bucket-truck purchase and keep the £6,000 in cash
Plan to rent a line robot as soon as one is sold
Steer her sister Amira towards face-to-face work at college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build something, if you're quick. On the forum I'd write about how small contractors could pool money for robots. At work I'd tell Dennis to start learning the tablets now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is about right for me. I'd start my firm in three years, before AGI in 2031, and have about three years after that before robots, so six years of building a name. When the robots come in 2034, I'd want to be the small firm that already knows how to use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the firm in year three with one second-hand truck and one other lineworker. I'd use AI for every quote and every safety plan from the start, so my office costs are tiny. And I'd do a short robotics course, so I'm not relying on a salesman to tell me what the machines can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. It's a race I think I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about small firms pooling money for robots. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four or five small contractors share one robot and book it by the week, like farmers share a combine. Nobody can afford a robot alone at first, but together you could. It's not a union, it's a business deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The power company could sign one big contract with a robot firm and shut us all out. That's the risk. I'd want my name known for storm work, because in a storm they take every crew they can get.

say: Five years is **enough to build** something if you're quick.
Small contractors could **pool money** to share robots.
think: Starting the firm before **2031** gives her six years of building a name.
When robots come in **2034**, she wants to already know how to use them.
do: Start the firm in **year three** with one truck and one lineworker.
Use **AI for every quote** and safety plan to keep office costs tiny.
Take a short **robotics course** so salesmen can't mislead her.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way, like a **race** she can run.
S3.quote: Four or five small contractors share one robot and book it by the week, like farmers share a combine.
fieldNote: Fatima frames shared robot ownership as **business, not a union**.
Her main fear is the power company signing **one big robot contract**.
She sees **storm work** as a niche that keeps small crews in demand.

steps.text: Launch her firm in year three with one used truck
Run every quote and safety plan through AI from day one
Take a short robotics course before buying any machine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it can't complain later. I'd say it to the apprentices and to my sister. On the forum I'd probably start a thread on how to plan a small firm around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this is the one where I win. I'd have my firm by thirty, two trucks by thirty-three, and a robot or two by the late 2030s. I'd be thirty-nine when the robots are as good as people, and I'd be the owner, not the hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the firm on my original five-year plan, with no rush. I'd buy a small flat once the firm is earning, so Amira has somewhere stable while she starts out. And I'd keep a close eye on robot makers, buying shares in one or two once I understand them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really. It's the same end point, but I'd be on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the owner, not the hand. What about the people who work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. I'd want to keep my crew on as robot minders and storm hands, but if the robot is cheaper, the market will push me. I'd try to be fair, and pay them well while I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything in this picture still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting married, a bit. My mum keeps asking, and I keep saying after the business. With ten years, I'd probably have to give her an answer before the robots arrive.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, and anyone who wastes it can't complain later.
I'd start a **forum thread** on planning a small firm around it.
think: This is the one where I **win**, with two trucks by thirty-three.
At **thirty-nine** I'd be **the owner**, not the hand.

fieldNote: Fatima expects to **own machines** rather than compete with them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it comes before I've built anything. What would help is banks lending to small trade firms for robots, the same way they lend for trucks, and the power company keeping some contracts open for small local crews.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the machines. Everyone asks if a robot will take my job, but the better question is whether someone like me can own the robot. Or is it only the giant firms?

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if a robot will take my job, but the better question is whether someone like me can own the robot.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old contract lineworker** on port upgrades and national storm call-outs, saving for her own firm.
She uses AI **every day** and sees it taking office work as a chance for small firms.
In fast AGI she is **anxious**, because robots arrive before she has built anything.
With more time she plans to **own robots** and share them with other small contractors.
Her outlook is **market-minded**: she blames no one and leans on family advice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive before her firm exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Bank loans** for small trade firms to buy robots, like truck loans.
Power company contracts kept open for **small local crews**.
